explanations: The defect is in Inventory::reserve in src/inventory.rs. available is an AtomicU32, and fetch_sub is applied before the stock check. When qty exceeds the current stock, the counter wraps around to a value near u32::MAX until the compensating fetch_add runs. In that window another thread's reserve sees a huge 'previous' value, passes the previous < qty check, and succeeds, so more units are sold than exist (and available() can briefly report about four billion units). The reservation must be conditional, for example a compare_exchange / fetch_update loop that uses checked_sub and only stores when enough stock remains.

fetch_update is implemented as a load followed by a compare_exchange_weak loop. If the compare-exchange fails because the value changed, the closure is called again with the fresh value. Here the closure is a pure computation (saturating_add then min), so repeating it is safe. There is no lock (first choice), a contended update is retried rather than dropped (third), and there is no fixed per-thread ordering (fourth). The let _ = only discards the Result, which can be Err only if the closure returns None, and this one always returns Some.

The loop reserves line by line. On the first error it releases every line already in reserved and returns OrderError::Stock. Because the counters are decremented immediately rather than checked up front, other threads can observe the temporarily lowered availability of the first SKU, and could be refused stock that is about to be returned. The first choice is wrong because the rollback happens inside place_order. The second is wrong because reserved borrows from lines, which outlives the loop. The third is wrong because each reserve call modifies its counter right away.

An atomic RMW such as fetch_add is indivisible and all operations on one atomic share one modification order, so no two callers can receive the same previous value. The Ordering argument only controls how this operation orders surrounding reads and writes of other memory. The second choice confuses ordering with atomicity. The third is wrong: reservations on different SKUs run concurrently and do not serialize callers. The fourth is wrong because uniqueness does not depend on the integer width or the absence of contention.
